note:
The household of John Leo Lewenz at 7 Clumber Crescent South (#80) on the 1921 return, transcribed by A. Hagues. All seven are bound by number and none is created; each was already in the record as a person and none carried a 1921 census row.

**The house comes from the schedule itself.** This is the one household on the crescent that the 1921 return numbers, and it gives 7. Richard Challands is returned at 7 Clumber Crescent South in 1911 and Wright's Directory prints 'Challands Mrs. S. E' on the crescent in 1913-14 and 1915-16, so the Challands household precedes the Lewenz one here.

**He did not stay.** His obituary, 'Prominent city business man: death of Mr. J. Leo Lewenz', gives his address at death as 21 Newcastle Drive, and A. Hagues dates that death to 1941. So this house is a stage in his life, not the end of it, and the Newcastle Drive address belongs to a later record rather than to this one. **No resident link to 21 Newcastle Drive is made here**, because the house he died in is not evidenced by this schedule.

**From the obituary.** He was born in Nottingham in 1867 and educated at Nottingham High School and in London. He joined Simon May and Co. Ltd, lace manufacturers of Nottingham, at a time when Jacob Weinberg, who founded the business, and Pius Lewenz, his own father, were partners. In 1887 he became associated with the firm's Calais branch and built it into the leading export house there, returning to Nottingham in 1918. He was chairman of the company from the death of Paul Meyer in 1928, and on his fiftieth anniversary with the firm in 1934 his fellow directors gave him a portrait in oils by the Nottingham artist N. Denholm Davis. He sat on the council of the Chamber of Commerce, was a member of the Reform Club and of the Jewish community, was an accomplished musician and accompanist, and collected historical works.

**Two threads worth pulling.** Jacob Weinberg, named in the obituary as the founder of Simon May and Co., is very probably the Weinberg the record already holds at 4 North Road in 1911 - if so, two heads of the same lace firm were living in The Park. And Pius Lewenz, his father, is not in the record at all. Neither link is made here; both want evidence of their own.

**An architect is staying in the house.** Herbert Hardy Wigglesworth, 54, born in Belfast, is returned as a visitor and gives his occupation as architect, employer. He is not otherwise in the record and is **not** assumed to have worked in The Park; but a visiting architect is worth checking against the estate's buildings and against the directory watch list.

Ages are as the enumerator wrote them, so a birth year worked back from one may be a year out either way.

Supporting: the 1911 return for 7 Clumber Crescent South; Wright's Directory of Nottingham 1913-14 and 1915-16, Clumber Crescent South.

people.bio: Lace and curtain merchant, and a leading figure in the Nottingham export trade. Born in Nottingham in 1867 and educated at Nottingham High School and in London, he joined Simon May and Co. Ltd, lace manufacturers, while its founder Jacob Weinberg and his own father Pius Lewenz were partners in it. From 1887 he was associated with the firm's Calais branch, which under him became the leading export house in that town, and he returned to Nottingham in 1918. He became chairman of the company on the death of Paul Meyer in 1928, and in 1934, on his fiftieth anniversary with the firm, his fellow directors presented him with a portrait in oils by the Nottingham artist N. Denholm Davis. He served on the council of the Nottingham Chamber of Commerce, where his experience of currency questions was particularly valued, and belonged to the Reform Club and to the city's Jewish community. He was an accomplished musician and accompanist with wide interests in the sciences and arts, and a student of history who built an extensive collection of historical works. He was living at 7 Clumber Crescent South in 1921 and at 21 Newcastle Drive at his death.
